options: Turns distinct row values into column headers, aggregating as it goes
Joins two unrelated tables together
Sorts a table by multiple columns
Removes duplicate rows from a result set
questions.explain: PIVOT rotates data from a 'tall' shape (many rows) into a 'wide' shape (fewer rows, more columns).

questions.q: What are the three things PIVOT requires?
options: A WHERE clause, a GROUP BY, and an ORDER BY
An aggregate function, a spreading column (FOR), and an explicit value list (IN)
A primary key and a foreign key
Two tables and a JOIN condition
questions.explain: AVG(ListPrice), FOR Color, and IN ([Red],[Blue],[Black]) are the three required pieces in the example.

questions.q: Why must the values in PIVOT's IN (...) list be named explicitly?
options: IN (...) is optional and can be omitted entirely
The values are generated automatically from GROUP BY
PIVOT does not automatically discover distinct values — you must specify which ones become columns
PIVOT can only handle numeric values in that list
questions.explain: Unlike DISTINCT-based grouping, PIVOT needs the exact set of values you want turned into columns spelled out.

questions.q: Why does the PIVOT example use an inner SELECT as its source instead of the raw table?
options: PIVOT cannot reference a table directly under any circumstances
The inner SELECT removes NULL values automatically
PIVOT needs a source narrowed to the relevant columns — pivoting directly on a table with unrelated columns causes confusing results
Inner SELECTs are required syntax for any PIVOT statement, regardless of columns
questions.explain: Narrowing to just ProductSubcategoryID, Color, and ListPrice avoids unrelated columns interfering with the pivot.

questions.q: Why are square brackets used around [Red], [Blue], [Black] in the PIVOT syntax?
options: Ordinary T-SQL identifier-quoting, letting a value like Red be used as if it were a column name
They indicate the values should be excluded from the result
They mark the values as string literals instead of identifiers
They are required only for numeric values
questions.explain: Since PIVOT turns these values into actual column headers, they need to be quoted as identifiers, same convention seen with reserved-word column names.
